blocks.html: Look at the end of a drawing pencil and you will find a code such as 2H, HB or 4B. The code tells you how hard the pencil's core is, and so how light or dark its line will be.

H stands for hard. B stands for black, and B pencils are soft. HB sits in the middle; most writing pencils are HB. F (for fine) sits between H and HB. The full range runs from about 9H, the hardest and lightest, to about 9B, the softest and darkest.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: Six grades and the lines they make with the same pressure. Lines get darker from the hardest (6H) to the softest (8B).

blocks.html: For H pencils, a bigger number means harder and lighter. For B pencils, a bigger number means softer and darker. So 6H is lighter than 2H, and 6B is darker than 2B.

A pencil "lead" is not lead. It is graphite mixed with clay and baked. More clay makes a harder core that leaves less graphite on the paper: a lighter, crisper line that keeps its point. More graphite makes a softer core that leaves more behind: a darker line that smudges and wears down faster.

blocks.title: Compare two grades
blocks.q: Which pencil makes the lighter line, a 6H or a 2H?
steps: Both are H pencils, so the number counts hardness.
The bigger number, 6H, is harder.
A harder core leaves less graphite, so its line is lighter.
blocks.a: The 6H.

blocks.html: Many people think a 6H is darker than a 2H because 6 is bigger than 2. For H pencils it is the other way around: the bigger the number, the harder and lighter. Check by asking which letter you have. H numbers go up toward light; B numbers go up toward dark.

blocks.html: Paper is not as smooth as it looks. Its surface has tiny bumps called tooth. When you draw, the tooth scrapes graphite off the pencil and holds it. Paper with more tooth grabs more graphite or charcoal; smoother paper takes fine lines and ink well.

blocks.html: Two erasers do most of the work. A kneaded eraser is a soft putty you can shape. Press it on the paper and lift: it picks graphite up without rubbing, so you can lighten a tone a little at a time. Stretch and fold it to clean it. A vinyl eraser is firmer. It removes marks more completely and leaves crisp edges.
Lighten by dabbing with a kneaded eraser. Remove lines and clean edges with a vinyl eraser, and always erase gently.

Hard scrubbing roughs up the paper fibers and flattens the tooth. Graphite then catches unevenly on the damaged patch, so new shading there looks blotchy and dark. Gentle erasing keeps the surface ready for more drawing.

blocks.title: Too dark
blocks.q: Rosa shaded a shadow too dark. She wants it one step lighter, not gone. What should she do?
steps: She wants to lighten, not remove.
A kneaded eraser lifts a little graphite each time it is pressed and lifted.
Dab, check, and dab again until the value is right.
blocks.a: Dab it with a kneaded eraser.

blocks.html: Scrubbing hard with an eraser damages the paper, and later shading looks patchy there. Erase gently, and use dabbing to lighten. If a spot still will not come clean, it is often better to work it into the drawing than to scrub a hole.
An eraser is also a drawing tool. Shade a soft gray tone, then lift out light shapes with a kneaded eraser: clouds, highlights, a shine on a cup.

blocks.html: How you hold the pencil changes the lines you can make. There are two main grips, and good artists switch between them many times in one drawing.

items: Writing grip: the pencil held near the point, as for writing. Your fingers move. It gives control for small, careful marks: eyes, letters, the edge of a leaf.
Overhand grip: the pencil held farther back, under your palm, with the lead lying more on its side. Your arm moves. It gives long, loose lines and broad, even shading with the side of the lead.

blocks.html: Hold near the point and move your fingers for small details. Hold farther back and move from the elbow or shoulder for long lines and big areas of tone.

Every stroke swings around a pivot. Fingers pivot at the knuckles, so they make short marks. The wrist makes medium curves. The elbow and the shoulder are far from the point, so they can sweep long, smooth lines and gentle curves that fingers cannot make in one stroke.

blocks.title: Shading the sky
blocks.q: Omar wants to shade a large, even sky behind a house. Which grip and which motion work best?
steps: The area is large and the tone should be even.
The side of the lead covers more paper with each stroke.
Moving from the elbow keeps strokes long and smooth.
blocks.a: The overhand grip, with the side of the lead, moving from the elbow.

blocks.title: Tiny details
blocks.q: Grace is drawing the stitches on a shoe. Which grip?
steps: Stitches are small and need control.
Holding near the point gives the most control.
blocks.a: The writing grip, near the point.

blocks.html: Many beginners draw everything with a writing grip and a still wrist. Their lines come out short, stiff and hairy, made of many little strokes. For long edges, lift your hand off the paper, hold the pencil farther back, and let your whole arm move.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace each line in one smooth stroke, moving your arm, not just your fingers. Print the sheet to practice on paper.

blocks.html: Sit up or stand back from the paper, and tilt it toward you on a board or an easel. Paper lying flat on a table is seen at a slant, and drawings made on it often come out stretched.

blocks.html: Graphite is only one way to draw. Three other media are worth knowing early, because each behaves differently.

items: Charcoal is soft, black and smudgy. Vine or willow charcoal is light and dusts off easily, so it is good for laying in a drawing. Compressed charcoal has a binder: it is darker and harder to erase. Charcoal pencils give more control for details.
Ink is permanent once dry. You cannot erase it, so you build tone with lines and dots: hatching, cross-hatching and stippling.

Colored pencil builds color in light layers. Several colors layered lightly mix on the paper. Pressing hard at the end (burnishing) gives a smooth, shiny finish, but then the paper will take few more layers. It is hard to erase fully.

blocks.html: Charcoal is dark and smudges; ink cannot be erased; colored pencil goes on in light layers.

Each medium sits on the paper in its own way. Charcoal is loose powder caught in the tooth, so a finger or a sleeve can move it. Ink soaks into the fibers and dries there. Colored pencil is pigment in wax or oil, and each layer partly fills the tooth until the paper is full.

blocks.title: Planning an ink drawing
blocks.q: Jon wants to draw a tree in ink. How should he start?
steps: Ink cannot be erased, so mistakes stay.
Light pencil lines can be erased.
He draws the tree lightly in pencil, inks over the lines he wants, waits until the ink is fully dry, then erases the pencil.
blocks.a: Sketch lightly in pencil first, then ink.

blocks.html: People expect charcoal to erase cleanly and ink to be fixable. Charcoal smears and leaves a gray ghost; ink stays. With charcoal, rest your hand on a scrap of paper. With ink, plan in light pencil first.

blocks.html: Line weight is how thick and dark a line is. Line quality is how the line behaves along its length: whether it swells and thins, stays smooth and sure, or breaks into many hairy little strokes. In the last unit you learned to make long, confident lines. Now you will learn where to make them heavy and where to keep them light.

blocks.name: ar-lines
blocks.cap: The same mug drawn twice. Drawing A uses one weight everywhere. Drawing B varies the weight.

blocks.html: Use heavier lines for near edges, the shadow side, the edge in front where two forms overlap, and the bottom where an object sits. Use lighter lines for far edges, the lit side and small details.

Varied weight copies what your eyes see. Edges on the shadow side look darker. Near things look sharper and stronger than far things. And where one form overlaps another, a heavier line on the front edge tells the eye which one is in front, even before you add any shading.

blocks.title: Two apples
blocks.q: One apple sits in front of another and overlaps it. Which edge gets the heavier line: the front apple's edge where it crosses the back apple, or the back apple's edge?
steps: Where forms overlap, the edge in front should read first.
A heavier line comes forward.
blocks.a: The front apple's edge.

blocks.title: Far mountains
blocks.q: Leo draws a field with mountains far behind it. Should the mountains' outline be heavier or lighter than the fence in front?
steps: Far things look softer and paler than near things.
A lighter line pushes the mountains back.
blocks.a: Lighter.

blocks.html: When every line has the same weight, a drawing looks flat, like a page in a coloring book. Before you finish, ask three questions: Where is the light? What is in front? What sits on the ground? Then go over those edges with heavier lines.

opts.task: Trace the oval lightly. Pretend the light comes from the upper left. Go over the lower right edge with a heavier line, and leave the upper left light.

blocks.cap: Practice: one shape, two weights.

blocks.html: A contour line follows an edge of a form. It is not only the outline around the outside. A contour drawing also follows the edges inside: a fold in a sleeve, the rim of a cup, the place where a finger overlaps another finger.

Contour drawing is slow on purpose. Let your eye creep along an edge, and let the pencil creep along the paper at the same speed, as if it were touching the object. Look at the object much more than at the paper.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: A contour drawing of a cup follows the outside, the far rim and the opening, and the inside edge of the handle.

blocks.html: A contour drawing follows every edge you can see, outside and inside, slowly, with your eyes on the object.

When you draw from memory, your hand draws a symbol: the idea of a cup or a hand. Following real edges slowly makes you notice the true shapes in front of you, which are almost never the symbol. That noticing is the heart of drawing from life.

blocks.title: Your own hand
blocks.q: You draw a contour of your hand resting on the table. Name three inside edges you could include.
steps: Look for edges that are not on the outline.
The creases at the knuckles, the edges of the fingernails, and the line where one finger overlaps the next are all edges.
blocks.a: For example: knuckle creases, fingernail edges, and overlapping fingers.

blocks.html: Many people draw only the outside outline, which looks like a cookie-cutter shape. Inner edges are what make a drawing look solid. Check by asking: where does one part meet another, fold over, or turn away?

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Put a mug, a shoe or your other hand in front of you. Draw its contour slowly, about as fast as an ant walking along the edge. Include at least three inside edges.

blocks.cap: Practice: a slow contour drawing.

blocks.html: A contour drawing of a crumpled paper bag is a classic exercise: it has many inside edges and no "right" shape to remember.

blocks.html: A blind contour is a contour drawing made while you look only at the object, never at the paper. You draw slowly, in one continuous line if you can, and let your hand follow your eye.

items: Choose something with interesting edges: your hand, a plant, a shoe.
Turn your chair so you cannot see the paper, or hold a paper plate over your drawing hand.
Set a timer for two to five minutes.
Put your eye on one point of the edge and your pencil on the paper. Move both together, slowly, until the time is up.

blocks.html: In a blind contour you never look at the paper. The goal is slow, careful looking, not a good-looking picture.

When you can see the paper, you start correcting the drawing toward what you expect. Taking the paper away leaves only the object. Your eye and hand learn to move together, and you notice small changes of direction you would have skipped.

blocks.title: A lumpy shoe
blocks.q: Kai's blind contour of his sneaker is lumpy, and the lines do not meet where they should. Did the exercise fail?
steps: A blind contour is judged by the looking, not the result.
If Kai followed the edges slowly and looked only at the shoe, he did the exercise right.
blocks.a: No. Odd-looking results are normal; slow looking is the point.

blocks.html: Many people think a blind contour that looks odd is a failure, and they start to peek. Its purpose is training the eye, not making a picture. A strange-looking result usually means you really did look at the object instead of the paper.
A modified contour lets you glance at the paper only to place your pencil when you lift it, then look back at the object. It is a step between blind contour and ordinary drawing.

opts.task: Draw your free hand without looking at the screen. Keep your eyes on your hand for the whole drawing, then look.

blocks.html: A contour line follows an edge. A cross-contour line runs across a surface, following its curve, like the stripes on a beach ball, the rings on a tree trunk or the lines of latitude on a globe.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: The same circle with two kinds of lines. Only the curving lines make it look round.

blocks.html: Cross-contour lines curve with the surface. On a flat surface they run straight; on a round surface they bend.

A straight line says "flat." A line that bends says "this surface curves away from me." When the stripes around a can bow downward, you see that you are looking down on it, because the near side of each ring sits lower on the page than the far side.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Rings around a can follow the shape of its top and bottom ellipses.

blocks.title: Stripes on a can
blocks.q: You draw a soup can seen from a little above, and want stripes around it. Which way should each stripe bend?
steps: You see the can from above, so its bottom edge is a curve bowing downward.
Stripes go around the can just like the bottom edge does.
blocks.a: Each stripe bows downward, matching the curve of the bottom.

blocks.html: Many people draw cross-contour lines straight across a round form, and it turns flat. Before you draw a line across a surface, trace the surface in the air with your finger and feel how it bends.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Hatching that follows the form (right) is called contour hatching. It uses the same idea for shading.

opts.task: Trace the circle, then draw five stripes that wrap around it like a beach ball. Make the middle stripe curve the least.

blocks.cap: Practice: turn a circle into a ball with lines alone.

blocks.html: A gesture drawing is quick: from about thirty seconds to a few minutes. It does not try to get the details right. It catches the movement, the weight and the direction of a pose: a cat stretching, a friend leaning on a wall, a dancer about to turn.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: A clothed mannequin with its line of action, the dashed curve. Move the slider to bend the pose.

blocks.html: Start with one line of action: a single curve through the whole pose. Then hang the head, chest and hips on it. Details come later, or not at all.

A drawing with good movement can always be given details. A stiff drawing full of details is hard to bring to life afterward. The short time limit forces you to look at the whole pose at once instead of one part at a time.

blocks.title: A stretching cat
blocks.q: A cat arches its back in a long stretch. What do you draw first?
steps: Find the biggest movement in the pose.
Here it is the long curve of the back, from the head to the tail.
Draw that curve first, then add the legs as simple lines.
blocks.a: The long curve of its back: the line of action.

blocks.html: Many people start a gesture with an outline or a face. In thirty seconds that leaves a careful head with no body. Start with the line of action through the whole pose, then add the big masses.

items: Good subjects: people at a park or a game, family members doing chores, pets, figures in a video you pause.
Draw many short poses: ten drawings of one minute each teach more than one drawing of ten minutes.
Use loose, light lines from the elbow.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Set a timer for one minute. Draw a person or a pet in motion: line of action first, then head, chest and hips. Clear the pad and do it again.

blocks.cap: Practice: one-minute gestures.

blocks.html: We draw people clothed in this course. Gesture works just as well with clothes on; folds often show the movement clearly.

blocks.html: Everything in a picture is either positive space or negative space. Positive space is the object itself: the chair, the mug, the plant. Negative space is the space around it and between its parts: the gaps between chair legs, the hole inside a mug handle, the sky between branches.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Is it a vase, or two faces looking at each other? The same edge belongs to both the positive and the negative shapes.

blocks.html: Negative shapes share their edges with the object. Draw the gaps correctly and the object comes out correct too.

You know what a chair is, so your hand wants to draw your idea of a chair. You have no idea of "the shape between the rung and the seat," so you have to look at it. Gaps are often simple shapes, such as rectangles and triangles, which are easier to judge than the object.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: A chair in gray. The lettered dots all sit in negative space: between the rails, between the seat and the rail, under the seat, and around the chair.

blocks.title: A mug handle
blocks.q: Your drawing of a mug handle looks wrong, but you cannot tell why. What can you look at instead?
steps: The handle is positive space. The hole inside it is negative space.
Compare the shape of the hole: is it tall or wide, round or like a letter D?
Fix the hole and the handle is fixed with it.
blocks.a: The shape of the hole inside the handle.

blocks.html: Many people ignore the gaps, such as between chair legs or under an arm. Those shapes are easier to judge than the object itself. When something looks off, check the negative shapes beside it.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Look at a chair, a stool or a plant. Draw only the shapes of the gaps, as if they were solid. Then shade the gaps dark. The object appears in the white you left.

blocks.cap: Practice: draw the spaces, not the thing.

blocks.html: A shape is flat. It has height and width, like a circle cut from paper. A form is solid. It has height, width and depth, like a ball. You met shapes in the Young Artists course; now each one grows into a form.

head: Shape (flat)
Form (solid)
In the world

a can, a pencil, a tree trunk
blocks.cap: Four shapes and the forms they become.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: A cylinder: from the side its outline is a rectangle, but light and the curved ends show its depth. Drag to move the light.

blocks.html: A shape has height and width. A form has height, width and depth. Circle to sphere, square to cube, triangle to cone, rectangle to cylinder.

Almost every object can be built from a few forms, so if you can draw these four, you can start almost anything. Two tools turn a flat shape into a form on paper: lines that show depth (like the ellipse at the top of a can) and shading that shows light turning across the surface.

blocks.title: An orange
blocks.q: You draw a circle for an orange. What makes it read as a sphere instead of a flat circle?
steps: A circle is a shape; it has no depth.
Shading from light to dark across it, a highlight and a cast shadow show that it is round and solid.
blocks.a: Shading: light on one side, shadow on the other, and a cast shadow.

blocks.title: Name the form
blocks.q: A drinking straw: which form?
steps: It is long and round, with circles at each end.
blocks.a: A cylinder.

blocks.html: People often use "shape" and "form" as the same word. In art, a shape is flat and a form is solid. A square drawn on paper is a shape; a box you could hold is a form.

blocks.html: The box is the most useful form in drawing: books, houses, tables and cars all start as boxes. Here is a simple way to draw one at an angle.

items: Draw the nearest vertical edge first, the corner closest to you.
Draw the two bottom edges going back from it, one to the left and one to the right.
Draw the far vertical edges, a little shorter than the near one.
Close the top with edges that match the bottom ones.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Three boxes. A and B look like boxes. C looks warped, because its edges spread apart as they go back.

blocks.html: Edges that are parallel on the real box either stay parallel or come together as they go back on paper. They never spread apart.

Things farther away look smaller. So the far end of a box looks a little smaller than the near end, and its edges lean toward each other. For a small box, the change is tiny and parallel edges look fine. But nothing gets bigger as it moves away, so edges that spread apart always look wrong. In perspective you will see exactly where receding edges meet.

blocks.title: Checking a box
blocks.q: Ana drew a box, and its back edge is longer than its front edge. What is wrong, and how can she fix it?
steps: The back edge is farther away, so it should look the same length or shorter.
She can shorten the back edge so the side edges stay parallel or come together slightly.
blocks.a: The back edge is too long; make it the same length or a little shorter.

blocks.html: People draw the back edges of a box farther apart than the front ones, so the box looks warped. Check each set of edges that go back into space. Hold a pencil along them: do they stay parallel or come together? If they spread apart, fix them.

blocks.html: A circle seen at an angle looks like an ellipse: a smooth oval, round at both ends. The top of a cup, the bottom of a bucket and a plate on a table are all circles you see as ellipses.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Plates at different heights. Near eye level a plate looks very thin. The farther above or below eye level, the rounder it looks.

blocks.html: An ellipse is thinnest near eye level and rounder the farther it is above or below eye level. It is smooth all the way around, with no points.

At eye level you see a plate exactly edge-on, so it is a line. Raise it or lower it and you start to see its face, so the ellipse opens up. The bottom of a cup on a table is farther below your eyes than its top, so you look down on it more steeply, and its ellipse is rounder.

blocks.name: draw-pics

caps: Right: smooth ellipses, rounder at the bottom

blocks.cap: Three cups. Only A has the ellipses right.

blocks.title: A glass on the table
blocks.q: You sit at a table and look at a glass. Which looks rounder: the ellipse at the rim, or the ellipse at the base?
steps: Both are below your eye level.
The base is farther below your eyes than the rim.
Farther from eye level means rounder.
blocks.a: The base.

blocks.html: People draw the bottom of a cup as a flat line, or give ellipses pointed ends like a football. A circle has no corners, so its ellipse has none either. And the bottom of a cup below eye level is rounder than the top, never flatter.

blocks.html: Complicated objects are built from simple forms. Artists call this construction: you find the boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones inside an object, draw them lightly, and then shape the real object around them.

head: Object
Forms inside it
rows: a cone (the shade), a cylinder (the stem) and a flat cylinder (the base)
a long cylinder and a cone at the tip
a cylinder, with a curved handle
a box with a roof on top
blocks.cap: Objects and their forms.

items: Look for the biggest form first.
Draw it lightly, with its ellipses or box edges.
Add the smaller forms where they attach.
Check sizes and angles against the object.
Shape the real outline, then erase the construction lines you do not need.
Add details last.

blocks.html: Big forms first, details last. Draw simple forms lightly, check them, then refine.

If the big forms are right, the details have a place to sit. If you start with a detail, every other part has to fit around it, and errors pile up. It is much easier to move a light cylinder than a finished, shaded handle.

blocks.title: A table lamp
blocks.q: In what order would you build a lamp with a cone-shaped shade, a thin stem and a round base?
steps: Find the biggest form: the shade, a cone.
Add the stem, a tall thin cylinder, below it, centered.
Add the base, a short wide cylinder, with an ellipse that matches its height below eye level.
Refine the outlines; add the switch and the cord last.
blocks.a: Shade, stem, base, then refine and add details.

blocks.html: People draw details first, such as the buttons on a phone or the eyes on a cat, and the overall shape never comes out right. Big forms first, details last. Draw construction lines lightly so they are easy to erase.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: Even a simple drawing goes in order: the big parts first, the small ones last. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Value is how light or dark something is. A white shirt has a light value; a black cat has a dark value. Value is separate from color: a yellow lemon and a pale blue sky can have nearly the same value.
A value scale is a strip of boxes that steps from white to black. Artists make them with 5, 7 or 9 steps. The white of the paper is the lightest step; your darkest dark is the last.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: A seven-step value scale, from white to black.

blocks.html: Value is lightness or darkness. A good value scale steps evenly: each box looks as different from its neighbors as every other box does.

Light falling on a form makes a range of values, from the brightest spot to the darkest shadow. A drawing that uses only a few middle grays looks weak; one that controls the whole range looks solid. Making even steps trains your hand to make exactly the value you mean.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Scale A steps evenly. Scale B makes the light steps too close together, then jumps to black.

blocks.title: A missing step
blocks.q: In a 5-step scale, the boxes are white, light gray, ?, dark gray, black. What value goes in the gap?
steps: The steps should be even.
Halfway between light gray and dark gray is a middle gray.
blocks.a: A middle gray.

blocks.html: People make the light steps too close together and then jump to black. Squint at your scale: if two neighbors blur together and one step jumps, redo the step that is off. Each step should look like the same jump.

blocks.html: Hatching makes value with lines. You draw many short parallel lines side by side. From a little distance, the eye blends them into a gray tone.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Three patches of hatching. The closer the lines, the darker the patch.

blocks.html: Lines closer together or heavier read darker. Keep the strokes in one area parallel.

A patch of hatching is part pencil and part white paper. More lines, or thicker lines, cover more of the paper, so less white shows through and the patch reads darker. That is all value is: how much light comes back from that spot.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Move the slider to make the hatching darker or lighter.

blocks.title: A hatched value scale
blocks.q: You want a 5-step scale using hatching only. How do the steps differ?
steps: Step 1 is the white paper.
Steps 2 to 5 use more and more lines, closer together (and a little heavier at the dark end).
Keep all the lines in one direction.
blocks.a: Each step has its lines closer together than the step before.

blocks.html: People hatch in every direction at once, and it looks scribbled. Keep the strokes in one patch parallel. Make each stroke with a quick flick from the wrist or elbow, lifting at the end.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: The left patch is hatching. The right one is scribbled.

blocks.cap: Fill each box with hatching only, lighter to darker. Print the sheet to practice with a pen or pencil.

blocks.html: Cross-hatching stacks layers of hatching. The first layer runs one way. The second crosses it at an angle. A third can cross both. Each layer makes the area darker.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: One, two and three layers of hatching.

blocks.html: Add a new layer only where the value should be darker. The lightest areas get no layers, middle values one or two, the darkest three or more.

Each layer covers more of the white paper, so the value steps down. Because you add layers only where they are needed, the light areas stay light. This is how artists shade with pens, which cannot press lighter or darker.

blocks.title: Shading a box
blocks.q: A box is lit from the left. Its top is the lightest side, its left side is middle, and its right side is the darkest. How many layers does each side get?
steps: The lightest side stays white or gets one light layer.
The middle side gets one or two layers.
The darkest side gets the most layers.
blocks.a: Top: none or one; left: one or two; right: three.

blocks.html: People cross every area at once, so there is no light left and the drawing turns into a dark net. Plan the light areas first and leave them alone. Add layers step by step, darkest areas last.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Move the slider: more layers, darker tone.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Leave the first box white. Give the next boxes one, two and three layers.

blocks.html: Stippling makes value with dots. Many dots close together read dark; a few dots far apart read light. It is slow, but it gives soft, even tones and a texture of its own.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Three patches of stippling.

blocks.html: More dots, closer together, read darker. Keep each mark a dot, not a dash.
Like hatching, stippling works by how much of the paper you cover. Dots have no direction, so a stippled area looks soft and smooth, which suits rounded forms, smooth fruit and soft shadows.

blocks.title: Darker without bigger dots
blocks.q: You want one area of a stippled drawing darker. What do you change?
steps: Value comes from how much paper is covered.
Add more dots there, closer together.
blocks.a: Add more dots, packed closer together.

blocks.html: People drag the pen and make little dashes instead of dots, which changes the texture and looks like hair or grass. Hold the pen upright and tap straight down, lifting it all the way between dots.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Dots (left) and dashes (right).

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Move the slider to add dots.

items: A fine pen works best; a sharp pencil works too.
Spread a light, even layer of dots over every area that is not pure white.
Go back and add more dots only where the value should be darker.
Leave the highlights as clean paper.
Be patient: even a small drawing takes many dots, so start with something the size of your palm.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Make a stippled value scale. Tap, do not drag.

blocks.html: Smooth tone is gray with no visible strokes, like a soft shadow on a wall. You build it slowly, with light, even layers.

items: Use small overlapping circles, or tight hatching that changes direction a little with each layer.
Keep the pressure light. Go over the area several times instead of pressing hard once.
For darker values, switch to a softer pencil (a 2B, then a 4B or 6B) instead of pressing harder.
To soften the tone, rub it gently with a blending stump (a rolled-paper stick, also called a tortillon) or a tissue.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Smooth tone, built from light layers. Move the slider to darken it.

blocks.html: Build smooth tone with many light layers. Get darker by adding layers and using a softer pencil, not by pressing hard.

Light layers leave graphite on the tops of the paper's tooth and let later layers fill in between. Heavy pressure crushes the tooth flat and polishes the graphite into a shiny skin. After that, new layers slide off, and the dark area looks shiny and patchy.

blocks.title: Stuck at medium gray
blocks.q: Mia pressed hard with an HB pencil. Her shadow is shiny and will not get darker. What should she do next time?
steps: Hard pressure burnished the paper, so it will not take more graphite.
She should use light layers, and switch to a softer pencil for the dark values.
blocks.a: Build light layers, and reach the darks with a softer pencil such as 4B or 6B.

blocks.html: People press hard to get a dark tone fast. Heavy pressure flattens the paper's tooth so later layers will not go on. Press lightly; let layers and softer grades do the work.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: A nine-step scale shows how gently smooth tone can change.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Fill the boxes with smooth tone, white to black, then check your scale.

blocks.html: Contrast is the difference between values that sit side by side. High contrast puts very light next to very dark. Low contrast keeps the values close together.
Key describes the overall value of a picture. A high-key picture is mostly light values, like a foggy morning. A low-key picture is mostly dark values, like a night scene.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: The same little landscape in a high key, a low key, with high contrast and with low contrast.

blocks.html: High contrast: very light beside very dark. High key: mostly light values. Low key: mostly dark values. Most strong drawings use the full range somewhere.

The eye goes first to the place of highest contrast, so artists put their strongest light-against-dark where they want you to look. Key sets the mood: high key feels airy and gentle; low key feels quiet, dramatic or mysterious. Painters call strong light and dark modeling chiaroscuro, Italian for "light-dark."

blocks.title: A foggy morning
blocks.q: You want a drawing of a foggy morning. What key and contrast fit best?
steps: Fog makes everything pale.
It also softens the differences between values.
blocks.a: A high key with low contrast.

blocks.html: People stay in the safe middle grays, so the drawing looks washed out. Use the full range somewhere: the white of the paper for the brightest light and your darkest dark for the deepest shadow. Squint to check that both are there.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: Colors have values too. Tap "Show in gray" to see them.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a simple scene, such as a hill, a tree and the sky, on each side of the line: once in a high key, once in a low key.

blocks.cap: Practice: the same scene in two keys.

blocks.html: Before you shade anything, decide where the light comes from. Pick one light source, such as a window, a lamp or the sun, and keep it in the same place for the whole drawing.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: A ball lit from the upper left. Drag in the picture to move the light and watch the shadows swing to the other side.

blocks.html: With one light, every lit side faces the light, and every shadow side and cast shadow points away from it.

Light travels in straight lines from its source. Surfaces turned toward it catch the light; surfaces turned away do not. An object also blocks light from the surface behind it, so its cast shadow falls on the side away from the light. When every object follows the same rule, the drawing feels like one real place.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: Three objects on one table. The cylinder is lit from the other side, as if there were a second sun.

blocks.title: Which side?
blocks.q: The light comes from a window on the right. On which side of an apple is its shadow side, and which way does its cast shadow fall?
steps: The lit side faces the window, on the right.
The shadow side is the side turned away: the left.
The cast shadow also points away from the light: to the left.
blocks.a: Shadow side on the left; cast shadow to the left.

blocks.html: People shade each object on a different side, as if there were several suns. Before shading, draw a small arrow in the corner of the page that shows where the light comes from, and check every object against it.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a sun in one corner. Then draw a ball, a box and a can, and shade each one on the side away from your sun.

blocks.cap: Practice: one light for everything.

blocks.html: Light does not just make a round form "light on one side and dark on the other." It moves across the surface in a series of values that artists name. Learn them on a ball, and you can find them on an apple, a head or a vase.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: Three of the parts of light on a sphere, with its cast shadow on the table. Drag to move the light; the table below names every part.

head: Part
What it is
rows: the brightest spot, where the light reflects straight toward your eye
the middle values where the surface starts to turn away
the darkest band on the form, where the surface turns away from the light
a dim glow inside the shadow, bounced up from the table or nearby things
the shadow the form throws onto the table
the darkest line, right where the form touches the table
blocks.cap: The parts of light on a round form, from the light into the shadow.

blocks.html: From the light into the shadow: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, and the cast shadow on the ground. Reflected light is always darker than any value in the light.

The more directly a surface faces the light, the more light it receives. As a ball curves away, each part faces the light less, so the values step down until the core shadow, where the surface turns fully away. Past the core, light bounced from the table brightens the shadow a little. That bounce is weak, so reflected light stays a shadow value.

blocks.title: Darker or lighter
blocks.q: Which is darker: the reflected light, or the halftone?
steps: The halftone belongs to the light side.
Reflected light belongs to the shadow side.
Every value in the shadow is darker than every value in the light.
blocks.a: The reflected light.

blocks.html: People make the reflected light as bright as the lit side, and the ball looks like it glows or turns to glass. Reflected light is always darker than any value in the light. Check by squinting: the whole shadow side should read as one dark shape.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: Tap the letter on the core shadow, then tap Check.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Rembrandt's Self-Portrait (1659): light falls on one side of the face, and the rest turns into soft shadow.

blocks.html: A cast shadow is the shadow an object throws onto the surface behind or beneath it. It is one of the strongest clues that an object sits in a real space.

blocks.name: draw-pics

caps: Right: away from the light, touching

blocks.cap: Three balls lit from the upper left. Only A has a believable cast shadow.

blocks.html: A cast shadow falls away from the light. It touches the object where the object touches the surface, and it is darkest and sharpest there, getting softer as it goes out.

The object blocks light, so the shadow lies on the far side of the object from the light. Right at the contact, almost no light can reach, so that spot is darkest. Farther out, light from the edges of the source sneaks in around the object, which softens the shadow's edge. When the light is low, as in the evening, shadows stretch long.

blocks.title: An evening walk
blocks.q: At sunset the sun is low in the west. Which way do the shadows of trees point, and are they long or short?
steps: Shadows point away from the light: toward the east.
A low light hits objects from the side, so their shadows stretch out.
blocks.a: Toward the east, and long.

blocks.html: People leave a gap between an object and its shadow, so the object seems to float. The shadow touches where the object touches. Put the darkest dark right at the contact, then let the shadow lighten as it moves away.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: A box's cast shadow follows its shape. Drag to move the light.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a ball on a table with the light from the right. Add its cast shadow: touching the ball, darkest at the contact, softer at the end.

blocks.cap: Practice: anchor an object with its shadow.

blocks.html: Shading a ball puts everything from this unit together: one light direction, the parts of light, a cast shadow, and smooth tone.

items: Choose the light direction and draw a small arrow.
Draw a circle lightly, and the line of the table.
Find the core shadow: a curved band on the side away from the light, following the ball's shape.
Draw the cast shadow on the table, away from the light, touching the ball.
Fill the whole shadow side with one middle-dark tone.
Darken the core shadow band, and the contact point most of all.
Shade the halftones on the light side, getting lighter toward the light.
Leave the highlight white (or lift it with a kneaded eraser).
Lift a little reflected light inside the shadow, keeping it darker than the halftones.

blocks.name: draw-pics

caps: A ball: the core shadow is a band away from the light
A flat disc: a dark ring all around

blocks.cap: Two attempts at the same ball.

blocks.html: Shade the values in order around the ball: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, with the cast shadow on the ground.

A sphere turns away from the light gradually in every direction, so its values must change gradually too. The core shadow sits where the surface turns away from the light, which is a curved band on one side, not the outline. An outline-shaped ring tells the eye "flat edge," which is why the ringed ball looks like a coin.

People shade a dark ring all around the edge, which makes a flat disc with a dark outline. The core shadow is a band on the side away from the light. The edge facing the light stays light, and the outline can almost disappear there.

blocks.title: Check the order
blocks.q: Starting at the highlight and moving toward the shadow, which value comes right after the halftone?
steps: The order is highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light.
blocks.a: The core shadow.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: Compare your ball with this one. Drag to move the light.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Shade the circle into a ball, light from the upper left. Print the sheet to shade one with a pencil.

blocks.html: A box is not round. It is made of flat sides called planes, and each plane faces one direction. So each plane catches one amount of light.

blocks.name: draw-pics

caps: One value per plane: a crisp box
Blended across the edges: a soft lump

blocks.cap: Two shaded boxes. A keeps one value on each plane; B blends tone across the edges.

blocks.html: Give each flat plane one even value. The plane facing the light is lightest, the plane turned away is darkest, and the values change sharply at the edges.

Every point on a flat plane faces the same direction, so every point receives about the same light. At an edge, the direction changes all at once, so the value changes all at once too. A round form turns gradually, which is why only round forms get soft gradations.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: The same box under three lights. The plane that faces the light most directly is always the lightest.

blocks.title: Three planes
blocks.q: A box sits on a table, lit from the upper right. You can see its top, its left face and its right face. Which plane is darkest?
steps: The light is above and to the right.
The top faces up, toward the light, and the right face faces it too.
The left face is turned away from the light.
blocks.a: The left face.

blocks.html: People blend tone across the edges of a box as if it were round, and the box turns soft and lumpy. Keep each plane one value, with crisp changes at the edges. A plane may darken a little toward its far end, but keep the jump at every edge.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: Drag to move the light and watch each plane change as a whole.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a box below the horizon. Pick a light, then give its three planes three different, even values.

blocks.cap: Practice: three planes, three values.

blocks.html: Proportion is how the sizes of parts compare. A drawing can be any size on the page and still look right, as long as its parts compare the way they do in real life. That is the same idea as a ratio, which you may know from the Math Ladder's Ratios topic.

Artists measure with a unit: one part of the object used as a ruler for the rest. "The bottle is four caps tall." "The window is two panes wide." Then they draw the unit and lay it off on the paper the same number of times.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: A bottle measured in units of its cap: four caps tall.

blocks.html: Choose one part as a unit, count how many units long the other parts are, and keep those counts the same in your drawing.

Your memory exaggerates the parts you care about and shrinks the rest. A measurement does not. Counting in units keeps the relationships true even when your drawing is bigger or smaller than the object, because a ratio does not depend on size.

blocks.title: Draw the bottle
blocks.q: A bottle is 4 caps tall. In your drawing, the cap is 2 cm tall. How tall should the whole bottle be?
steps: The bottle is 4 caps tall.
Each cap is 2 cm in the drawing.
blocks.a: 8 cm.

blocks.title: Going backward
blocks.q: A lamp is 3 shade-heights tall. You drew the whole lamp 15 cm tall. How tall should the shade be?
steps: The lamp is 3 shades tall.
So one shade is the whole height divided by 3.
blocks.a: 5 cm.

blocks.html: People draw parts at the size they feel they are, such as a big face and small hands, instead of the size they measure. Before you draw a part, ask "how many units is it?" and count.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: Proportion in people: figures measured in head heights. These are averages artists use; real people vary.

blocks.html: You will use head heights for faces and figures later in this course: Figure Proportions in Heads.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Drawing"

blocks.html: Sighting is measuring with your pencil. It lets you compare sizes on an object across the room, so you can find its proportions.

items: Hold the pencil at arm's length, with your elbow straight.
Close one eye.
Hold the pencil upright for heights or level for widths, flat to your face (not tipped toward or away from you).
Line up the tip with one end of a part, and slide your thumb to the other end. That length is your unit.
Without changing anything, move the pencil to another part and count how many units long it is.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: The thumb marks one unit on the pencil, here the bottle's cap. The bottle measures three units.

blocks.html: Keep the elbow straight and one eye closed, mark a unit with your thumb, and compare other lengths with it. Use the counts, not the sizes, on your paper.

A sighting only works if the pencil is the same distance from your eye every time. A straight elbow is an easy way to make sure it is. Closing one eye keeps you from seeing two pencils. The numbers you get are ratios, so you can draw at any size: if the cup is 2 units tall and 3 wide on the pencil, it is 2 by 3 on your paper too, in any unit you like.

blocks.title: A window
blocks.q: Sighting a window, you find its width is 2 thumb-lengths and its height is 3 of the same lengths. You draw the window 10 cm wide. How tall should it be?
steps: Height : width = 3 : 2.
The drawing is 10 cm wide, so one unit is $10 \div 2 = 5$ cm.
Height = $3 \times 5 = 15$ cm.
blocks.a: 15 cm.

blocks.html: People bend the elbow between measurements, which moves the pencil closer or farther and changes the scale, so every comparison is wrong. Lock your elbow every time, as if your arm were a stick.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Sight a mug or a book near you. How many widths tall is it? Draw it on the grid using that count.

blocks.cap: Practice: draw what you measured.

blocks.html: Sighting also measures angles and alignments. The trick is to hold the pencil perfectly vertical or perfectly horizontal, so you have something steady to compare the object with.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: An edge compared with a level pencil (the dashed line). The gap between them shows the angle.

items: Angles: hold the pencil level (or upright) at arm's length, in front of a slanted edge such as a roof line. See how far the edge tilts away from the pencil, then draw the same tilt.

Alignments: hold the pencil straight up and down. It becomes a plumb line, named after a weight on a string that hangs straight down. Look at what lines up along it: which point sits directly above which.

blocks.name: draw-pics
blocks.cap: A plumb line through P, the left edge of the cup's rim. Point B, the cup's bottom corner, lies straight below it.

blocks.html: Hold the pencil truly vertical or horizontal, never tilted to match the edge. Compare the edge with it to judge the angle, and use it as a plumb line to see what lines up.

Our eyes judge angles badly on their own, but they compare two lines side by side very well. A level or upright pencil gives you a fixed reference. Some people also think of a clock face: an edge tilting up to the right like a clock hand pointing at two o'clock rises at about 30 degrees.

blocks.title: A roof
blocks.q: You hold your pencil level in front of a roof. The roof edge rises from the level pencil about one third of the way to straight up. About what angle is that?
steps: Straight up from level is 90 degrees.
One third of 90 is 30.
blocks.a: About 30 degrees.

blocks.html: People tilt the pencil to match the edge, which tells them nothing: an edge always matches itself. Keep the pencil truly level or truly upright, and compare.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Look at a table or a door at an angle. Use a level pencil to judge one slanted edge, then draw it at that tilt.

blocks.cap: Practice: draw an angle you measured.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Plumb bob"

blocks.html: The grid method copies a picture one square at a time. You draw a grid over the picture (or on a clear sheet laid on it) and a matching grid on your paper. Then you copy what is in each square into the matching square.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: A small picture with a 4 by 4 grid, copied into a bigger 4 by 4 grid.

blocks.html: Both grids need the same number of rows and columns and the same shape of square. Bigger squares on the paper enlarge the drawing by the same factor.

A grid breaks one big, hard problem into many small, easy ones. Each square holds only a few lines, and their positions inside the square are easy to see: "the ear starts halfway across the top." It is also a scale drawing: if each square is 3 times as wide, everything in the drawing is 3 times as wide.

blocks.title: Enlarging
blocks.q: A photo has a grid of 2 cm squares. You draw a grid of 6 cm squares on your paper. The photo is 10 cm wide. How wide will your drawing be?
steps: The scale factor is $6 \div 2 = 3$.
The drawing is 3 times as wide as the photo.
$3 \times 10 = 30$ cm.
blocks.a: 30 cm.

blocks.title: Counting squares
blocks.q: A photo 8 cm wide and 12 cm tall gets a grid of 2 cm squares. How many squares are there?
steps: Across: $8 \div 2 = 4$ columns.
Down: $12 \div 2 = 6$ rows.
$4 \times 6 = 24$ squares.
blocks.a: 24 squares.

blocks.html: People draw a paper grid with a different shape than the picture's grid, such as squares on the photo but rectangles on the paper. That stretches the drawing. Use squares on both, with the same number of rows and columns. Label the rows and columns so you do not lose your place.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Copy a simple picture square by square. Print the grid to use on paper; draw grid lines lightly so they erase.

blocks.html: After a while, your eyes get used to your drawing and stop seeing its mistakes. Artists use a few tricks to see it fresh.

items: Step back. Put the drawing up and look from across the room. Proportions and big shapes show at a distance.
Squint. Half-close your eyes. Details blur away and only the big light and dark shapes remain, so you can check your values against the object.
Flip it. Look at the drawing in a mirror, or hold the paper up to a light and look from the back. Crooked and lopsided shapes jump out when the image is reversed.
Turn it upside down. The subject stops looking familiar, so you see shapes and angles instead.
Measure. Use sighting and plumb lines to test one part against another.
Take a break. Come back after a few minutes with fresh eyes.

blocks.html: Step back, squint for the big values, and flip the drawing in a mirror to catch crooked or lopsided shapes.

Your brain quickly learns a picture and starts filling in what it expects to see. Changing the view, by distance, blur, a mirror or turning, takes away that expectation, so the drawing looks new and its errors show.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: Squinting helps you judge contrast. Which picture has strong lights and darks, and which is all middle gray?

blocks.title: A lopsided vase
blocks.q: Sam's vase looks fine to him, but his friend says it leans. Which check will show it best?
steps: A lean is a lopsided shape.
Flipping the image in a mirror shows lopsided shapes clearly.
A plumb line through the vase's center also tests whether it is upright.
blocks.a: Look at it in a mirror (or test it with a plumb line).

blocks.html: People keep their nose close to the paper. Many errors only show from a distance or flipped. Build the habit: every ten minutes or so, stand up, step back and look.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a mug from life. Then step back, squint and compare. Fix one thing you notice.

blocks.cap: Practice: draw, then check.

blocks.html: Paper is flat, yet a good drawing can look deep, as if you could walk into it. You already built solid forms in Drawing a Box. Now we place those forms in space. Three simple cues do most of the work, and you can use them without any rulers.

items: Overlap. A thing in front hides part of the thing behind it.
Size. Things farther away look smaller, even when they are the same real size.
Placement. Below your eye level, things farther away sit higher on the page. (Above eye level, like clouds or birds, farther things sit lower.)

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Three depth cues: overlap, smaller size and higher placement.

blocks.html: Overlap, smaller size and higher placement tell the eye that something is farther away. Use them together and the picture looks deep.

Your eye judges distance from clues. A near tree covers part of a far one, so the far one must be behind it. Light from a far object reaches your eye at a smaller angle, so it takes up less room in your view, and the ground farther away rises toward the horizon in your view. A drawing that copies these clues fools the eye the same way.

blocks.title: Three trees in a field
blocks.q: Three trees of the same real size stand at different distances. How do you draw the farthest one?
steps: Farther things look smaller, so draw it the smallest.
The trees stand on the ground below eye level, so the farthest one sits highest on the page.
If it is behind another tree, let the nearer tree overlap it.
blocks.a: Smallest, highest on the page, and partly hidden if something is in front.

blocks.html: A common beginner drawing puts a far house the same size as a near one, side by side on one bottom line, like stickers on a shelf. Nothing tells the eye which is farther. Check: is the far thing smaller, higher, and behind something?

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Picture A has no depth cue: the trees are the same size on one line. B and C each use one cue.

blocks.html: Later in this unit you will meet two more depth tools: the lines of linear perspective, and the paler, softer look of atmospheric perspective.

blocks.html: Every perspective drawing starts with one line: the horizon line. It is not just where the land happens to end. It is the height of the viewer's eyes, called eye level.
The horizon line is always at eye level. Things below it show their tops; things above it show their bottoms; things that cross it show neither.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Drag the horizon line up and down. The box below it shows its top; the box above it shows its bottom.

blocks.html: Stand at the beach and look at the sea. However tall you are, the far edge of the water seems to sit right at your eye height. Climb a dune and the horizon rises with you; sit in the sand and it drops. So the horizon line in a drawing tells us where the viewer's eyes were. A table top below your eyes shows its top surface. A shelf above your eyes shows its underside.

blocks.title: Indoors
blocks.q: You sit at a desk and draw your room. Where does the horizon line go?
steps: Indoors you cannot see the real horizon, but you still have an eye level.
Look straight ahead: the height of your eyes on the far wall is the horizon line.
Draw it there, even though no line is painted on the wall.
blocks.a: At your eye level on the far wall.

blocks.title: Changing the view
blocks.q: In a drawing, the horizon line sits very low, near the bottom of the page. What does that tell you?
steps: The horizon is the viewer's eye level.
A low eye level means the viewer is low: sitting, lying down or a small child.
Most things will be above eye level, so we look up at them and see their bottoms.
blocks.a: The viewer is low and looks up at most things.

blocks.html: Many people think the horizon line is wherever the land meets the sky. In hilly places or indoors, the land does not show eye level. Find eye level instead: look straight ahead without tilting your head. That height is your horizon line, even in a room.
In Showing Depth you saw that far things below eye level sit higher on the page. Now you know why: they climb toward the horizon line.

blocks.html: Stand in the middle of a straight road or a long hallway and look ahead. The sides seem to come together far away. In a drawing, that meeting place is the vanishing point, and it sits on the horizon line.

When you face a box straight on, its front is a flat rectangle: its horizontal edges stay horizontal, and its vertical edges stay vertical. Only the edges that go back, away from you, slant. All of them aim at the same single point. This is one-point perspective.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Drag the vanishing point (the pink dot) or the horizon line and watch the boxes change.

blocks.html: In one-point perspective, every edge that goes straight back from you meets at one vanishing point on the horizon line. Edges across and up and down stay horizontal and vertical.

Parallel lines going away from you never meet in real life, but the space between them takes up a smaller and smaller angle of your view as they go farther. Far enough away, the gap shrinks to nothing: that is the vanishing point. Lines that go straight away from you all shrink toward the point straight ahead of your eyes, which is on the horizon line.

blocks.title: Draw a box
blocks.q: How do you draw a box in one-point perspective?
steps: Draw the horizon line and put one vanishing point on it.
Draw the front of the box as a plain rectangle.
From each corner, draw a light line toward the vanishing point.
Decide how deep the box is and draw the back edges parallel to the front edges.
Erase the extra parts of the guide lines.
blocks.a: A box whose back edges all aim at one point.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw boxes above, below and across the horizon line. You can print the sheet.

blocks.html: Two common slips: edges that go back but miss the vanishing point (the box looks twisted), and a vanishing point placed above or below the horizon line. Check with a ruler: extend each back edge. All of them should cross at one point, and that point should sit on the horizon line.
Leonardo da Vinci used one-point perspective in The Last Supper: the lines of the ceiling and the side walls lead back toward a point at the head of the central figure.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Last Supper. Look for the lines of the ceiling and walls and follow them back.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Vanishing point

blocks.html: One-point perspective is not only for boxes. Roads, railroad tracks, hallways, rows of trees and the inside of a room seen straight on all use it. You already know the rule from One-Point Perspective: lines that go straight back meet at the vanishing point.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: A road, its center dashes and a row of posts, all going back to one point.

blocks.html: There is a second idea here that surprises people. Fence posts that are equally spaced on the ground do not look equally spaced in a drawing. The gaps shrink as they go back, and the posts get shorter.
Lines that go straight back meet at one vanishing point, and equal spaces on the ground look shorter and shorter as they go back.

How big something looks depends on how far away it is. A post twice as far away looks about half as tall. The same is true of the gaps between posts: the far gaps are farther from you, so they look smaller. That is why railroad ties seem to crowd together near the horizon.

blocks.title: Fence posts
blocks.q: A fence post 10 meters away is drawn 6 cm tall. An identical post stands 20 meters away. About how tall should you draw it?
steps: Its distance doubled, from 10 m to 20 m.
Drawn size goes down in step with distance: twice as far looks about half as big.
Half of 6 cm is 3 cm.
blocks.a: About 3 cm.

blocks.title: A room
blocks.q: You stand in a doorway and look straight into a room. Where do the lines where the walls meet the floor and ceiling go?
steps: Those lines go straight away from you.
In one-point perspective, lines going straight back meet at the vanishing point.
The vanishing point is on the horizon line, at your eye level on the far wall.
blocks.a: To one vanishing point at your eye level on the far wall.

blocks.html: People space railroad ties or fence posts evenly on the paper. That makes the road look like it tilts up like a wall. Let each gap be a little smaller than the one in front of it, and let the posts shrink as they go back.
Canaletto painted views of Venice in careful perspective. In this one, the long rows of arches along the square lead your eye back to the far end.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Square of Saint Mark's, Venice, by Canaletto.

blocks.html: The geometry behind "twice as far looks half as big" is in the Math Ladder's Similar Figures.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Vanishing point
Grokipedia: Perspective (graphical)

blocks.html: Turn a box so that one corner points at you. Now no face is flat to you. The edges on the left side go back to the left, and the edges on the right side go back to the right. That takes two vanishing points, both on the horizon line: two-point perspective.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Drag the horizon line and the two vanishing points. Watch the box stretch when the points come close together.

blocks.html: In two-point perspective, a box seen corner-first has two vanishing points on the horizon line, one for each side. Vertical edges stay vertical.

A box has three sets of parallel edges. In one-point perspective, two sets (across and up-down) are flat to you, so only one set needs a vanishing point. Turn the box and the across edges now go away from you too, to the left and to the right, so they need a second point. The up-down edges are still flat to you while you look straight ahead, so they stay vertical.

blocks.title: A building on a corner
blocks.q: You stand on a street corner and look at a building's corner. How do you set up the drawing?
steps: Draw the horizon line at your eye level, about the height of a person's eyes on the building.
Put one vanishing point far to the left and one far to the right on that line.
Draw the nearest corner as one vertical line.
From its top and bottom, draw lines to each vanishing point. Add the far vertical edges.
blocks.a: A corner line, two vanishing points far apart, vertical edges kept vertical.

blocks.html: Placing the two vanishing points close together makes boxes look stretched and sharp-cornered, as if seen through a fisheye lens. Put them far apart, often off the edges of the paper. Tape scrap paper beside your drawing so you have room.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw a box corner-first. Imagine two vanishing points near the left and right edges of the pad.

blocks.html: In Caillebotte's Paris Street; Rainy Day, the building at the corner of the two streets shows two sides going back in different directions.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Paris Street; Rainy Day, by Gustave Caillebotte.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Vanishing point
Grokipedia: Perspective (graphical)

blocks.html: In two-point perspective the vertical edges stay vertical. That is true when you look straight ahead. But tip your head back to look at the top of a skyscraper, and the sides of the building seem to lean in toward each other high above you. Now even the vertical edges meet, at a third vanishing point.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Looking up at a tall box: the vertical edges meet at a third point high above.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Looking down from up high: the vertical edges meet at a third point below.

blocks.html: Three-point perspective adds a third vanishing point for the vertical edges: above the object when you look far up (a worm's-eye view), below it when you look far down (a bird's-eye view).

Vertical edges stay vertical only while they are flat to you, which happens when you look straight ahead. Tilt your view up or down and those edges now go away from you too. Any set of parallel edges that goes away from you meets at its own vanishing point.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: You draw a tall tower from its base, looking almost straight up. How many vanishing points?
steps: The two sides of the tower go back left and right: two points on the horizon.
You look far up, so the vertical edges also go away from you.
They meet at a third point high above.
blocks.a: Three.

blocks.html: Some people add a third vanishing point to every drawing to make it look advanced. For an ordinary eye-level view of a house or a box, the vertical edges should stay vertical. Save three-point for views that look far up or far down.
Photographs of tall buildings taken from the street often show the sides leaning inward, like the Chrysler Building seen from below.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Chrysler Building, New York.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Vanishing point
Grokipedia: Perspective (graphical)

blocks.html: Look at hills or buildings far away on a hazy day. The nearest ones are dark, sharp and full of color. Each row farther back looks paler, bluer and softer, until the farthest almost melts into the sky. Artists call this atmospheric perspective (or aerial perspective).

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Hills fading into the distance.

blocks.html: Faraway things look lighter, bluer or grayer, softer at the edges, lower in contrast and less detailed than near things.

Between you and a far hill is a great deal of air, with tiny bits of water and dust. They scatter light. Some of the sky's blue light is scattered toward you from all that air, which veils the hill in pale blue, and the hill's own darks and details get washed out. The more air in between, the stronger the veil.

blocks.title: Push it back
blocks.q: You want a tree in your drawing to look far away. What do you change?
steps: Draw it smaller and higher on the page (the depth cues from earlier).
Use lighter values and less contrast: no deep blacks.
Keep the edges soft and leave out small details like single leaves.
blocks.a: Smaller, lighter, softer and simpler.

blocks.html: A common mistake is drawing far hills with the same dark lines and crisp detail as the foreground. They then jump forward. Save your darkest darks, sharpest edges and finest details for the front.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: The mistake: every hill the same dark green. The picture looks flat.

blocks.html: Leonardo da Vinci wrote about this effect in his notes on painting, and the hazy blue landscape behind the Mona Lisa is a famous example. Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow shows it in winter: the far valley and mountains are much paler than the dark figures and trees in front.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Hunters in the Snow, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

blocks.html: With pencil alone, atmospheric perspective is all about value: see Contrast and Key.

blocks.html: Composition is how you arrange things in the picture. The same tree can make a dull picture or a lively one depending only on where you put it.

The rule of thirds is a simple starting tool. Divide the picture into thirds across and thirds down, like a tic-tac-toe grid. Placing the main subject near one of the lines, or where two lines cross, often looks livelier than placing it dead center. A horizon on the upper or lower third line usually looks better than one that cuts the picture exactly in half.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: A tree near the left third line, the horizon near the lower third line. The buttons show other guides.

blocks.html: Divide the picture into thirds both ways. The subject near a third line or a crossing, and the horizon on a third line, often look more lively than dead center. It is a guideline, not a law.

A subject in the exact center feels settled and still, and a horizon in the middle splits the picture into two equal halves that compete. Off center, the spaces are uneven, and uneven spaces move the eye around the picture. The name "rule of thirds" was first printed in 1797 by the English artist John Thomas Smith, in a book about drawing landscapes.

blocks.title: Finding the lines
blocks.q: Your paper is 30 cm wide and 21 cm tall. Where are the third lines?
steps: Across: 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so vertical lines at 10 cm and 20 cm from the left edge.
Down: 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so horizontal lines at 7 cm and 14 cm from the top.
blocks.a: Vertical lines at 10 and 20 cm; horizontal lines at 7 and 14 cm.

blocks.title: Sky or ground?
blocks.q: In a landscape, the horizon sits on the upper third line. What does the picture show more of?
steps: Above the upper third line is one third of the picture: the sky.
Below it are two thirds: the land.
blocks.a: More land than sky.

blocks.html: Some people treat the rule of thirds as a law and think a centered subject is always wrong. It is not. Portraits, symmetrical buildings and calm scenes are often centered on purpose. Use thirds when you want movement and centering when you want stillness, and choose on purpose.
Ruisdael's Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede sets its low horizon well below the middle, so the big sky and the windmill fill most of the picture.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede, by Jacob van Ruisdael.

blocks.html: When you look at a picture, your eye lands somewhere first. That spot is the focal point. In a good drawing, the artist decides where it is. You have already met two tools that help: the rule of thirds for where to put it, and contrast from Contrast and Key.

items: Contrast: the strongest light against the darkest dark.
Detail: the most careful, finished part of the drawing.
Isolation: one thing standing apart from a group.
Leading lines: roads, edges or gazes that point to it.
Difference: the one thing that is a different shape, size or color.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: A boat at sea. Which spot does your eye find first?

blocks.html: The focal point is where the eye goes first. Make it with the strongest contrast, the most detail, isolation, lines that lead to it, or a difference from everything around it.

The eye is drawn to change: an edge where dark meets light, a place with many small shapes, something that does not match its neighbors. If everything has the same contrast and detail, there is no change to find, and the eye wanders without resting.

blocks.name: draw-focal
blocks.cap: Contrast: the one dark circle pulls the eye.

blocks.name: draw-focal
blocks.cap: Isolation: the circle that stands apart pulls the eye.

blocks.title: A portrait
blocks.q: You are drawing a person's portrait. Where should the focal point be, and how do you make it?
steps: Usually the face, and often the eyes, should be the focal point.
Put your darkest darks and lightest lights near the eyes.
Draw the eyes with the most care, and keep the clothes and background simpler and softer.
blocks.a: At the eyes, made with the most contrast and detail.

blocks.html: People often draw every part with equal detail and equal contrast: every leaf, every brick, every fold. The picture looks busy and the eye has nowhere to rest. Choose one place to finish fully and let the rest be simpler.

blocks.html: A picture can feel steady or feel like it is tipping over. Artists talk about visual weight: big, dark, busy or brightly colored shapes feel heavy; small, light, plain ones feel light. Balance is how that weight is spread around the picture.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance.

items: Symmetrical balance: the two halves mirror each other. It feels calm and formal.
Asymmetrical balance: different things on each side still feel even, like a big light shape on one side and a small dark one on the other.
Radial balance: things spread out from a center, like a flower, a wheel or a rose window.

blocks.html: Symmetrical balance mirrors the halves; asymmetrical balance evens out unlike things; radial balance spreads from a center.

Think of a seesaw. Two equal children balance at equal distances: that is symmetry. A small child can balance a bigger one by sitting farther out: that is asymmetry. In a picture, a small dark shape near the edge can balance a large pale shape near the middle. Nothing is weighed; it is how heavy each part looks to the eye.

blocks.title: Even it out
blocks.q: A big dark tree fills the left side of your landscape, and the right side is empty sky and field. How can you balance it without a second big tree?
steps: A big dark shape is heavy.
A smaller shape with strong contrast or interest can balance it from farther out.
Put a small dark house, a bird or a bright sun on the right side.
blocks.a: Add a small but strong shape on the right side.

blocks.html: Many people think a picture balances only when both halves match. Matching halves are one kind of balance, but most lively pictures use asymmetrical balance: unequal things that still feel even.
Color and Design has more on balance as a principle of design.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, grades 6 to 8 (Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas and work)
Grokipedia: Symmetry

blocks.html: Some lines in a picture act like arrows. A road, a river, a fence, the edge of a table or a row of trees carries the eye along it. These are leading lines. Used well, they lead the viewer to the focal point.

blocks.name: draw-lead
blocks.cap: A road and a fence leading to the house, and a river leading out of the picture.

blocks.html: Leading lines such as roads, rivers, fences, edges and the direction a person looks carry the eye through the picture, best of all toward the focal point.

The eye follows edges and directions. A line that starts near the bottom edge of the picture and travels inward pulls the eye in with it. Lines do not need to be drawn as lines: a row of fence posts, a gaze from one person to another, or a pointing hand makes an implied line the eye follows just the same.

blocks.title: Where does it lead?
blocks.q: A path starts at the bottom corner of your drawing and curves toward a cottage near the right third line. What does the path do for the picture?
steps: The eye enters where the path meets the edge.
It follows the curve.
It arrives at the cottage, the focal point.
blocks.a: It leads the viewer into the picture and to the cottage.

blocks.html: A strong line that runs straight out of the picture, like a road shooting off the side edge, takes the viewer's eye out with it. Bend it back toward the subject, end it at the focal point, or stop it with a tree or a turn.
The road in Roads, Rooms and Rails is a leading line too: it goes straight to the vanishing point.

blocks.html: Before a big drawing, many artists make a few thumbnails: tiny, quick sketches, often only a few centimeters wide, that try out different arrangements. Each takes a minute or two. You are not drawing details, only big shapes and the light and dark pattern.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: Three thumbnails of one idea. Which arrangement do you like best?

blocks.html: Small, quick thumbnails let you try several arrangements and crops before the real drawing. A viewfinder helps you choose the view.

Fixing a composition in a small sketch takes a minute; fixing it in a finished drawing can mean starting over. Small sketches also hide details, so you see only what matters for composition: big shapes, balance, where the focal point sits and where the horizon falls.

A viewfinder is a card with a rectangle cut out of it, the same shape as your paper. Hold it up and look through it to frame the scene. Move it closer to your eye to take in more; move it away to crop in tight.

blocks.title: Make a viewfinder
blocks.q: Your paper is 12 inches wide and 9 inches tall. You cut a viewfinder opening 4 inches wide. How tall should the opening be?
steps: The opening must have the same shape as the paper: the same ratio of width to height.
The paper is 12 by 9; dividing both by 3 gives 4 by 3.
So the opening is 3 inches tall.
blocks.a: 3 inches.

blocks.html: Many people start the final drawing at once and only discover the composition problems, like a subject jammed against the edge or a horizon cutting the page in half, when the drawing is almost done. Spend five minutes on three thumbnails first.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Sketch a quick thumbnail here: big shapes only. Then try another arrangement.
