blocks.html: A still life is a drawing of objects that do not move: fruit, cups, bottles, books, a vase. It is one of the best ways to practice, because your subject waits patiently while you study its shapes, its shading and its shadows. The setup matters as much as the drawing.

items: Group the objects; let some overlap.
Vary heights and sizes: something tall, something medium, something small.
Leave uneven gaps and set some objects farther back than others.
Light from one side with a single lamp or a window, so each form has a clear light side, shadow side and cast shadow.

blocks.name: draw-still
blocks.cap: A grouped setup lit from the side, and a row of objects.

blocks.html: Group the objects, overlap some, vary their heights, leave uneven gaps, and light them from one side.

Overlap and staggered depth give the eye depth cues. Different heights and uneven gaps make a more interesting shape for the whole group. A single light from the side gives each object a light side and a shadow side, which is what makes it look round or boxy. Light from straight above flattens forms and hides the shadows that describe them.

blocks.title: Fix the setup
blocks.q: Ava lines up an apple, a mug, a bottle and a box in a straight row, evenly spaced, under the ceiling light. What would you change?
steps: Group them: move the apple in front of the mug so it overlaps.
Put the tall bottle toward the back and the small apple toward the front.
Make the gaps uneven.
Turn off the ceiling light and use one lamp from the side.
blocks.a: Group and overlap them, stagger their depth and heights, and light them from one side.

blocks.html: The most common setup problem is a row: objects side by side, the same distance apart, often the same height, lit from straight above. It looks like a shelf in a store, and the drawing comes out flat. Before you draw, make a thumbnail or two to test the arrangement.

blocks.name: draw-still
blocks.cap: Two more setups with a problem: all one height, and light from straight above.

blocks.html: Painters have arranged still lifes this way for centuries. Cézanne tipped and overlapped his fruit and baskets on purpose in The Basket of Apples.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Basket of Apples, by Paul Cézanne.

blocks.html: Texture is how a surface feels, or looks as if it would feel: furry, rough, smooth, grainy. In a drawing, texture comes from two things: the kind of mark you make, and the pattern of light and dark. You already have the marks from Cross-Hatching and Stippling.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Eight textures and the marks that make them.

blocks.html: Match the mark to the surface (short strokes for fur, long wavy lines for wood, dots for sand, crisp broken darks for rough stone) and show texture most where light grazes the surface.

A rough surface is a field of tiny bumps. When light skims across it from the side, each bump gets a lit side and a tiny shadow, so the texture shows strongly. Where the light hits straight on, or where the surface is in shadow, those tiny shadows disappear and the texture fades. Far away, the bumps are too small to see at all.

blocks.title: Drawing a tree trunk
blocks.q: How do you draw the rough bark of a tree trunk lit from the left?
steps: Use broken, vertical marks with small dark cracks.
Show the crisp bark pattern most along the edge where the light meets the shadow.
On the lit side, keep marks light and sparse; in the deep shadow, let the bark merge into a darker tone.
blocks.a: Broken vertical marks, strongest where light meets shadow, fading in the full light and the deep shadow.

blocks.html: People draw texture evenly over every part, like wallpaper. The object then looks flat and busy. Put the most texture where light grazes the surface and in the front, and let it fade in the light, in the shadow and in the distance.
Dürer's watercolor Young Hare shows how fur works: strokes follow the direction the fur grows, and the texture is strongest where light catches it.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Young Hare, by Albrecht Dürer.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw a small square of fur, a square of wood grain and a square of rough stone.

blocks.html: Matte things like an apple, a clay pot or a cotton shirt show soft light that turns gradually into shadow, as in Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light. Shiny and see-through things play by the same rules but look very different.

blocks.name: draw-surface
blocks.cap: A matte ball, a shiny ball, a glass drawn as it looks, and a glass outlined and filled gray.

items: Shiny: small, sharp, very bright highlights; strong contrast; crisp reflections of the window, the lamp and the table.
Glass: you see what is behind it, slightly bent or shifted, plus a few bright edge highlights and some dark edges.

blocks.html: Shiny things show sharp highlights and reflections with strong contrast. Glass shows what is behind it, slightly bent, plus a few bright and dark edges.

A matte surface scatters light in every direction, so its lit side looks evenly bright. A shiny surface reflects light mostly in one direction, like a mirror, so you see a crisp, bright image of the light source and of the room. Glass lets most light through, and its curved surface bends that light, which is why things behind a glass look shifted or enlarged. The Science Lab's optics page shows how light reflects and bends.

blocks.title: A glass of water
blocks.q: How do you draw a clear drinking glass on a striped tablecloth?
steps: Draw the ellipses of the rim and base and the sides, lightly.
Draw the stripes you see through the glass: they look shifted and wider.
Add the darker edges where the glass curves away from you.
Leave the paper white (or lift with an eraser) for a few crisp highlights on the rim and side.
blocks.a: Draw what you see through it and on it, not a gray glass shape.

blocks.html: People often outline a glass with a dark line and fill it with gray. Glass is not gray; it is mostly what is behind it. Draw the background through the glass, the edge darks and the bright highlights, and the glass appears.
Keep your brightest whites by planning them: leave those spots of paper untouched from the start, or lift them out at the end with a kneaded eraser.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Specular highlight
John Ruskin, The Elements of Drawing (1857), Letters I and II

blocks.html: Cloth looks hard to draw because it has so many folds. But folds are not random. They start where the cloth is held up, at a point of support such as a pin, a hook, a shoulder or a knee, and they spread away from it.

blocks.name: draw-cloth
blocks.cap: Cloth hanging from one pin and from two pins.

blocks.html: Find the points of support first. Folds start there and run away from them. Shade each fold like a small cylinder.

Gravity pulls cloth down, and only the supports hold it up. Hung from one point, the cloth falls away in a fan of folds that all radiate from that point. Hung from two points, it sags between them in U-shaped curves, and falls in fans below each point. Each fold is a rounded ridge, so it has a light side, a core shadow and a shadow side, just like the cylinder in Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light.

blocks.title: A towel on a hook
blocks.q: A towel hangs from a single hook. How do you start?
steps: Mark the hook: the point of support.
Draw the outside edges falling from the hook.
Draw a few main folds as lines spreading from the hook down to the hem.
Shade each fold: light on the side facing the light, darker on the turning side.
blocks.a: Start from the hook and let the folds radiate from it.

blocks.html: People draw folds as random lines scattered over the cloth. Random lines make cloth look crumpled or dirty. Ask where each fold comes from: every main fold should start at a support or at a place where the cloth bends.

blocks.name: draw-cloth
blocks.cap: Random lines go nowhere. On a bent sleeve, folds gather on the inside of the elbow.

blocks.html: Set up a dish towel pinned at one corner, then at two corners, and draw each for ten minutes. You will use this again in The Clothed Figure.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw cloth hanging from one pin. Start at the pin.

blocks.html: Faces are where drawings most often go wrong, because we think we know what a face looks like. A few averages, measured the way you learned in Proportion: Comparing Sizes, fix most problems. Real faces vary, so treat these as a starting map, then look at your model.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: An adult head seen from the front, with its guide lines.

items: The eyes sit about halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
The head is about five eye-widths wide, with one eye-width between the eyes.
The bottom of the nose is about halfway between the eyes and the chin.
The mouth is about one third of the way from the nose to the chin.
The ears run from about the brow line to the bottom of the nose.

blocks.html: On an adult head seen from the front, the eyes are about halfway down, the face is about five eyes wide, and the nose ends about halfway from the eyes to the chin.

We pay so much attention to eyes, nose and mouth that we picture them taking up most of the head. In fact the skull above the eyes is large, and the hair hides how tall it is. Measuring shows the eyes sit near the middle.

blocks.title: Placing the features
blocks.q: You draw a head 24 cm tall from the top of the skull to the chin. Where do the eyes, the bottom of the nose and the mouth go?
steps: Eyes: halfway down, so 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm from the top.
Nose: halfway from the eyes (12 cm) to the chin (24 cm), so 18 cm from the top.
Mouth: one third of the way from the nose (18 cm) to the chin (24 cm). That gap is 6 cm, and a third of it is 2 cm, so 20 cm from the top.
blocks.a: Eyes at 12 cm, nose at 18 cm, mouth at 20 cm.

blocks.html: Almost everyone places the eyes too high at first, which leaves a tiny forehead and a short skull, like a mask pasted on the front of the head. Check: measure from the top of the skull (not the hairline) to the chin. The eyes belong near the middle.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: In A the eyes are too high. In B they sit about halfway down.

opts.task: Drag the eyes, nose and mouth onto their lines, then tap Check.

blocks.html: An eye is not a flat almond with a circle inside. It is a ball sitting in a socket, and the lids wrap around it like a shell. Thinking of it as a ball, the way you shaded the sphere in Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light, makes eyes look real.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: Eye A floats in the white; in eye B the upper lid covers the top of the iris.

items: The upper lid covers the top of the iris (the colored part) when a person looks calm.
The upper lid casts a small shadow on the eyeball just under it.
The white of the eye is a ball, so it is shaded too: it is rarely as white as the paper.
The upper lid has the thicker, darker line; the lower lid is lighter.

blocks.html: An eye is a ball in a socket: the lids wrap around it, the upper lid covers part of the iris, and the upper lid casts a shadow on the eyeball.

The lids are thick skin that rests on a round ball, so their edges follow the curve of the ball. The upper lid sticks out a little and casts a shadow. A whole iris showing, with white all around it, happens only when the eyes are opened very wide, which is why it reads as startled or scared.

blocks.title: Drawing one eye
blocks.q: What order works well for drawing an eye?
steps: Draw the upper and lower lid lines lightly, curving around the ball.
Draw the iris as a circle, partly hidden by the upper lid.
Add the pupil and a small highlight, the same on both eyes.
Shade the top of the eyeball under the lid, and the corners.
Darken the upper lid line most.
blocks.a: Lids, iris under the lid, pupil and highlight, shading, then darker lines.

blocks.html: A common mistake is drawing the whole iris as a circle floating in the white. It makes the face look startled. Let the upper lid cover the top of the iris.
Eyelashes grow in clumps and point outward and down along the curve of the lid. Suggest them with the darker lid line and a few flicks at the outer corner rather than drawing every lash.

blocks.html: The nose and mouth stick out from the face, so light and shadow describe them better than outlines do. Start from the guide lines you placed in Proportions of the Head.

blocks.name: draw-nose
blocks.cap: Nose A has an outline all around. Nose B is drawn with its shadow side, the shadow under the tip and the nostrils.

items: The nose is like a wedge: a bridge, two sides, and a ball at the tip with the nostril wings beside it. With light from one side, one side of the wedge is in shadow, and there is a shadow under the tip.
The nostril wings are about as far apart as the inner corners of the eyes, on an average face.
The corners of the mouth line up roughly below the pupils.
With light from above, the upper lip is usually darker than the lower lip, because it faces down, away from the light.

blocks.html: Draw the nose with its planes and shadows, not a hard outline. The corners of the mouth line up roughly below the pupils.

There is no line around a real nose. What you see are planes turning away from the light: the shadow side of the bridge, the dark nostrils, the shadow cast under the tip. Draw those and the nose stands out from the face. An outline says "flat cutout," and the nose looks pasted on.

blocks.title: Where does the mouth go?
blocks.q: The bottom of the nose is 18 cm from the top of the head, and the chin is at 24 cm. Where does the mouth line go, and how wide is the mouth?
steps: The mouth sits about one third of the way from the nose to the chin: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so about 20 cm from the top.
Its corners line up roughly below the pupils.
blocks.a: About 20 cm from the top, with the corners below the pupils.

blocks.html: People outline the whole nose, both sides and the bottom, so it looks flat. Draw only the nostrils, the shadow under the tip and the shadow side, and leave the lit side open.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: use the guide lines to place a nose with shadows and a mouth with its corners under the pupils.

blocks.html: Most faces you draw will not look straight at you. When the head turns, the features move around the curve of the head like stickers on a ball. Three views matter most: front, three-quarter and profile (side).

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: The same head from the front, in three-quarter view and in profile.

items: In three-quarter view, the center line of the face curves around the head, and the far eye looks narrower than the near eye.
Less of the face shows on the far side; more of the cheek and ear shows on the near side.
In profile, the ear sits just behind the middle of the head, and the head (with the skull) is about as deep from front to back as it is tall.

blocks.html: When the head turns, the center line curves, the far eye looks narrower, and in profile the ear sits just behind the middle of the head.

A head is roughly a ball with the face on its front. Things on a ball that turn away from you are seen at a slant, so they look narrower; this is called foreshortening. The ear is on the side of the head, but the head is deeper than people think, and the skull behind the ear is large. That puts the ear behind the middle when you see the head from the side.

blocks.title: Three-quarter view
blocks.q: You draw a head turned partly to the left. How do you place the eyes?
steps: Draw the head shape and a center line that curves to the left of middle.
Place the eye line where it would be from the front, curving around the head.
Draw the near eye full width. Draw the far eye narrower, close to the center line, partly hidden by the bridge of the nose.
blocks.a: The far eye is narrower and close to the curved center line.

blocks.html: Two common mistakes: keeping both eyes the same width when the head turns, and putting the ear too close to the face in profile, which leaves almost no back of the skull. Check: in profile, find the middle from front to back; the ear starts just behind it.

blocks.html: An expression is not only a mouth. The eyebrows, the eyelids and the mouth move together. Change only the mouth and the face looks like a mask with a sticker on it.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: Six moods. Look at the eyebrows first, then the eyes and the mouth.

items: Happy: mouth corners up, cheeks lifted, eyes narrowed a little.
Surprised: brows raised high, eyes wide, mouth open.
Angry (cross): brows pulled down toward the nose, mouth tight and flat.
Sad: inner ends of the brows raised, mouth corners down.
Worried: brows tilted up in the middle, mouth uneven.
Sleepy: upper lids lowered, brows relaxed.

blocks.html: Eyebrows, eyelids and mouth change together: raised brows and an open mouth for surprise, lowered brows and a tight mouth for anger.

The muscles of the face are connected. A real smile lifts the cheeks, which pushes up the lower lids and narrows the eyes. Surprise raises the brows, which opens the eyes wide. People read faces quickly, and they read the eyes and brows as much as the mouth.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: Tap the moods and watch the brows and lids change, not just the mouth.

blocks.title: Read the face
blocks.q: A face has its brows pulled down and together, and the mouth pressed into a flat line. What does it show?
steps: Brows pulled down toward the nose: a frown.
A tight, flat mouth goes with it.
blocks.a: Anger (a cross face).

blocks.html: People change only the mouth and leave the brows and eyes the same. A smile with worried brows looks nervous, not happy. Draw the brows and lids first; they carry much of the feeling.
Try it in a mirror: make each face and watch what your brows and lids do.

blocks.html: Hands have a reputation for being hard, but they become manageable when you build them the way you built objects in Building Objects from Forms: big simple shape first, details last.

blocks.name: draw-hands
blocks.cap: Hand A is built from the mitten shape, with fingers of different lengths on a curve. Hand B is five equal sausages.

items: Start with the mitten: the palm and the fingers together as one shape, with the thumb as a separate wedge on the side.
The middle finger is about as long as the palm.
The fingers are different lengths: the middle finger is longest and the little finger shortest.
The knuckles line up on a curve, not a straight line, and the fingers fan out slightly from them.
Each finger bends in three places; the thumb joins the hand low on the side of the palm, near the wrist.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: The palm and the middle finger are about the same length; the knuckles make an arc.

blocks.html: Start with the mitten shape of the palm and fingers together. The middle finger is about as long as the palm, and the knuckles line up on a curve.

A hand is a box-like palm with jointed cylinders attached. Seeing the big mitten shape first gets the size and the gesture right before you divide it. The finger bones fan out from the wrist, so their knuckles form an arc, and that arc is why a fist or a relaxed hand curves.

blocks.title: Proportions
blocks.q: Your drawing of a palm is 8 cm long from the wrist crease to the knuckle of the middle finger. About how long is the middle finger?
steps: The middle finger is about as long as the palm.
So it is about 8 cm.
Make the index and ring fingers a little shorter and the little finger clearly shorter.
blocks.a: About 8 cm.

blocks.html: People draw five separate sausages of the same length, starting from a straight line. Fingers differ in length, the knuckles make an arc, and the thumb starts much lower on the hand. Check: does your middle finger stick out the farthest? Is the knuckle line curved?

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw your own non-drawing hand three times, first as a mitten, then dividing the fingers.

blocks.html: Your own hand is the most patient model you will ever have. Draw it relaxed, pointing and holding a cup.

blocks.html: Artists measure the body using the head as a ruler: the height from the top of the head to the chin. This is the same sighting idea you used in Sighting with a Pencil, applied to people. The numbers are averages that artists use; real people vary.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: An adult, a child of about six and a toddler, measured in head heights.

items: An adult is about 7½ heads tall. The halfway point is near the hips.
A teenager is about 7 heads.
A child of about six is about 6 heads.
A young child of about three is about 5 heads.
A toddler is about 4 heads.
With the arms hanging down, the elbows are near the waist and the wrists near the hips.

blocks.html: Artists measure the body in head heights: an adult is about seven and a half heads tall; a young child only four or five.
The head grows less than the rest of the body after birth, while the legs grow the most. So a small child has a big head for their size and short legs, and the body gets more "heads tall" with age.

blocks.title: Head size from height
blocks.q: You want to draw an adult figure 30 cm tall. About how tall is the head?
steps: An adult is about 7½ heads tall.
blocks.a: About 4 cm.

blocks.title: Height from head size
blocks.q: You drew a toddler's head 5 cm tall. About how tall is the whole toddler?
steps: A toddler is about 4 heads tall.
blocks.a: About 20 cm.

blocks.html: People draw a child as a small adult: a little head on long legs. Children have bigger heads for their size and shorter legs. Measure in heads before you draw details.

blocks.html: In Gesture Drawing you drew the movement of a pose in quick, loose lines. The line of action is the single most important of those lines: one curve that runs through the whole pose, from the head, down the body, to the foot that carries the weight.

blocks.name: draw-pose
blocks.cap: Four clothed mannequin figures with their lines of action.

blocks.html: Draw one curved line through the whole pose first. The head, chest and hips hang on it, and the figure gets its movement from it.

When a body moves, it bends as a whole: leaning, reaching or twisting, the spine curves and the weight shifts to one leg. A single curve captures that. Most lively poses follow a gentle C-curve (bending one way) or an S-curve (bending one way, then the other). A perfectly straight vertical line has no movement, which is fine for standing at attention and nothing else.

blocks.title: Start a pose
blocks.q: A person reaches up to a high shelf on their toes. How do you begin?
steps: Draw a long curve from the reaching hand down through the body to the standing foot.
Hang an egg for the head and boxes for the chest and hips on that curve.
Add the limbs last, following the stretch.
blocks.a: With one long curve from the hand to the standing foot.

blocks.html: People draw the body stiff and straight, like a stick figure at attention, even when the pose is moving. Exaggerate the curve a little; a pose drawn too straight always looks stiffer than the real one.

blocks.name: ar-proportion
blocks.cap: Move the slider to bend the pose and watch the line of action curve.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw ten lines of action in two minutes, each a different pose: leaning, reaching, kicking, sitting.

blocks.html: Artists often use a jointed wooden mannequin, or draw one in their heads, to work out a pose. You can draw any figure the same way, using the forms from Building Objects from Forms: an egg for the head, boxes for the chest and hips, cylinders for the arms and legs, and balls at the joints. Ours are dressed in plain clothes so you can see each part.

blocks.name: draw-pose
blocks.cap: A clothed mannequin figure and its forms.

blocks.html: Build the body from simple forms: an egg for the head, boxes for the chest and hips, cylinders for the limbs and balls at the joints. Limbs bend only at the joints.

Boxes and cylinders show which way each part faces and how it turns in space, which a flat outline cannot. And bones do not bend: an arm bends at the shoulder, elbow and wrist, a leg at the hip, knee and ankle. Marking each joint with a ball reminds you where the bends are allowed.

blocks.title: Build a pose
blocks.q: How do you draw a mannequin figure waving?
steps: Draw the line of action (see The Line of Action).
Place the egg head, the chest box and the hip box on it, tilted the way the body leans.
Put balls at the shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles.
Join the balls with cylinders. The waving arm bends at the elbow, not in the middle of the forearm.
blocks.a: Line of action, then the egg and boxes, then joints and cylinders.

blocks.html: People bend arms and legs between the joints, like rubber hoses. That looks boneless. Limbs bend only at the joints: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle.

blocks.name: draw-pose
blocks.cap: A bends at the elbows and knees. B bends like a rubber hose, with no joints.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw a mannequin standing, then the same mannequin waving.

blocks.html: Clothes hang on a body the way cloth hangs from pins in Folds in Cloth. The body is the support. So the order matters: first the gesture and the forms, then the clothes on top.

items: Draw the line of action and a light mannequin first.
Find the points of support: shoulders, elbows, waist, knees. Folds start there.
At a bent joint, folds bunch up on the inside of the bend and the cloth pulls smooth over the outside.
Loose clothes hang away from the body in long folds; tight clothes follow the forms underneath.

blocks.name: draw-pose
blocks.cap: Clothed figures: the clothes follow the body underneath.

blocks.name: draw-cloth
blocks.cap: A bent sleeve: the folds gather on the inside of the elbow.

blocks.html: Draw the gesture and forms first, then hang the clothes on them. Folds pull from the shoulders, elbows, waist and knees.

Clothes have no shape of their own. They take their shape from the body and from gravity. If you know where the body is, you know where the cloth is held up and where it hangs, and the folds make sense.

blocks.title: A person sitting with a jacket on
blocks.q: What order do you draw in?
steps: Line of action and the mannequin: the bent hips and knees, the arms resting.
The outer edge of the jacket, a little outside the body forms.
Folds where the jacket bends: inside the elbows and at the waist.
Shade the folds like small cylinders; add buttons, pockets and seams last.
blocks.a: Gesture, forms, outer shape of the clothes, folds, then details.

blocks.html: People draw the clothes first and the body underneath comes out the wrong size, with arms too short inside the sleeves or no room for the hips. Draw the mannequin lightly first, even when only the clothes will show.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Practice: draw a friend or family member sitting in a sweater for ten minutes, mannequin first.

blocks.html: Athletes stretch and musicians play scales before they perform. Drawing works the same way. A few minutes of simple marks loosens your hand and arm and wakes up your eye, so your first real drawing of the day is not wasted getting loose.

items: Straight lines: draw two dots and connect them in one smooth stroke. Move from the shoulder for long lines, not just the wrist.
Ghosting: before each line, move your pencil above the paper along the path two or three times, then draw it.
Circles and ellipses: rows of them, round and flat, as in Circles in Depth: Ellipses.
A value scale: five even steps from white to black, as in Value and the Value Scale.
A quick contour: one minute of blind contour of your own hand.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace the ellipses, then draw your own rows. Print the sheet to warm up on paper.

blocks.html: A few minutes of straight lines, circles, ellipses and value scales loosens the hand before a drawing.

Smooth, confident lines come from the whole arm moving freely. At first your hand is stiff and your marks are short and hairy. Warm-ups get the big muscles moving and remind your eye and hand to work together, the same way a runner jogs before a race.

blocks.title: A ten-minute warm-up
blocks.q: You have ten minutes before you start a still life. How could you spend them?
steps: Two minutes of straight lines between dots.
Three minutes of circles and ellipses.
Two minutes on a five-step value scale.
Three minutes of quick gesture or contour drawings of the objects.
blocks.a: Lines, ellipses, a value scale, then quick sketches of the subject.

blocks.html: People skip the warm-up and spend the first drawing of the day getting loose, then judge themselves by that stiff first drawing. Treat the first few minutes as practice that does not need to look good.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Warm-up value scale: fill the five boxes from light to dark, then check it.

blocks.html: The artists who improve fastest are rarely the ones with the most talent. They are the ones who draw often. A sketchbook makes that easy: one book you carry or keep near you, where every drawing goes, good or bad.

items: Draw a little most days: ten or fifteen minutes is enough.
Draw from life when you can: your shoes, a cup, a plant, a pet asleep.
Date every page so you can see your progress.
Keep everything. Do not tear out pages you dislike.
Mix quick sketches (a minute or two) with a few longer studies.

blocks.html: Short, regular practice adds up: draw a little most days, from life when you can, and date every page.

Skills grow from many repetitions spread over time, not from one long session now and then. Ten minutes a day for a week is over an hour of drawing, and the habit means you keep going. Dated pages also show you something you cannot feel day to day: how much you have improved.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: Ten minutes most days
Dating every page
Drawing your shoes or a cup from life
Waiting for a free afternoon
Tearing out pages you dislike
Drawing only when you feel inspired

blocks.cap: Sort each card, then tap Check.

blocks.title: Adding it up
blocks.q: Sam draws for 10 minutes on 6 days each week. How many minutes is that in 4 weeks?
steps: One week: 6 × 10 = 60 minutes.
Four weeks: 4 × 60 = 240 minutes, which is 4 hours.
blocks.a: 240 minutes (4 hours).

blocks.html: People wait for long free afternoons and then rarely draw. Ten minutes most days does more than a long session once a month.

Ideas for a page: everything on your desk, your hand in five poses, the view from a window, one object from three sides, people waiting at a bus stop (quick gestures, clothed and from a polite distance).

blocks.html: You can draw from real things in front of you (from life) or from photographs. Both are useful, and good artists use both. But a photo is not the same as what your eyes see, and knowing the differences keeps you from copying a camera's mistakes.

items: Life shows real depth: with two eyes and a moving head you understand the form. Light and shadow show their full range.
Photos hold still forever and capture moving things (a running dog, a wave, a bird), but they flatten form.
Phone cameras close to a subject bend it: a hand held toward the lens looks huge and a nose up close looks too big.
Photos often turn shadows solid black and bright skies pure white, losing details your eyes would see.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: You can walk around it to understand the form
It holds still while a bird is in flight
Shadows may turn solid black
You see depth with both eyes
Near things can look stretched and huge
The light may change as the sun moves

blocks.cap: Sort each card, then tap Check.

blocks.html: Life drawing shows real depth and light; photos flatten form and can bend near things. Use your own photos or free-to-use ones, and give credit.

Your eyes adjust as you look from bright to dark parts, so you see detail in both. A camera picks one exposure for the whole scene. A camera close to its subject also exaggerates whatever is nearest, because the near parts are so much closer to the lens than the far parts.

blocks.title: Whose photo?
blocks.q: You find a great photo of a horse online and want to draw from it. What should you check?
steps: Photos made by other people are usually protected by copyright.
Use your own photos, photos you have permission to use, or ones marked free to use (public domain or an open license).
Write the photographer's name with your drawing.
blocks.a: Check that you may use it, and give the photographer credit.

blocks.html: People copy photo distortions as if the eye saw them that way: a giant hand from a selfie, a face with a stretched nose, shadows filled in solid black. When something looks odd, ask whether it is the camera, and draw what the real thing looks like.
A good habit: draw from life most of the time, and use photos for moving subjects and for practice when life is not available. Check your work with the tools from Checking Your Drawing.
